claims.text: A parameter-free multiscale framework can decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The framework will improve thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy by about 20–30% over earlier models.
HfNbTaTiZr can be represented initially as a defect-free bulk crystal and modified with 1 wt.% oxygen to represent realistic conditions.
Anharmonic lattice dynamics, on-the-fly machine-learned force fields, and Green–Kubo calculations can be combined to compute lattice thermal conductivity.
DFT-derived electronic states and Boltzmann transport can be used to compute electronic thermal conductivity separately.
Explicit oxygen impurities can be incorporated to model defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The method is applicable below 200 K.
Experiments on HfNbTaTiZr show comparable lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions below 200 K.
An HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen has a measured total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions and oxygen-defect scattering mediate separation of phononic and electronic transport channels.
Eliminating Debye-temperature and ideal-crystal assumptions allows the framework to capture full anharmonic effects and realistic defect scattering.
Using DFT electronic structure with Boltzmann transport accounts for electronic-band-structure effects in electronic thermal conductivity.
Combining separately calculated lattice and electronic conductivities will produce more accurate total thermal-conductivity predictions.
At 300–1200 K, the summed prediction should fall within 10–17 W/(K m).
Below 200 K, the predicted lattice and electronic contributions should be roughly equal.

Earlier approaches relied on DFT-derived elastic properties, Debye-temperature assumptions, defect-free structures, or combined lattice and electronic effects, limiting their accuracy across the stated temperature range.
The framework is valid for HfNbTaTiZr containing up to about 1 wt.% oxygen and over temperatures extending from below 200 K to about 1200 K.
Below 50 K, additional quantum corrections may be required.
The exact accuracy gain is uncertain because of the interplay between anharmonicity and defect scattering, especially at extreme temperatures.
